analysis.title: Payrolls a signal of continued strong momentum
key_insights: October nonfarm payrolls beat all economist estimates. The report's key-points list gives 165k against a 70k estimate, while the body text gives 159k. The two figures conflict within the report.
Payrolls were revised up by 84k over the previous two months, the third month in a row with upward revisions.

The 6-month average payroll gain is 82k, below the pre-pandemic 180k-200k average. SEB attributes this to slower labour force growth from halted immigration and increased deportations. SEB puts the new break-even pace at about 50k and sees the current pace as slightly above it.

Gains were broader than in prior years. Manufacturing added 19k, transportation 25k and professional business services 70k. Leisure and hospitality fell 13k, the largest monthly decline. AI-exposed sectors were weaker in earlier months, but information (-1k) and finance (+7k) were not as weak in October.
Unemployment fell to 4.1% from 4.2%, helped by a recovery in participation and the labour force. SEB says this is in line with the Fed's view of the longer-run non-inflationary rate.

Hourly earnings rose 0.4% m/m and 3.1% y/y, above the 0.3% and 2.9% estimates. SEB says this is consistent with the inflation target given productivity growth of about 2% or slightly higher, so the labour market is not an inflation risk.
SEB expects another rate hike at the December Fed meeting and believes it will be the final one. The October data should not change that plan.

Next week's CPI is described as more important than the jobs data. The Fed is also watching equity markets and fading confidence in the AI expansion. SEB says it would take much steeper stock declines to stop a December hike, since a continued decline could make the Fed pause because of wealth effects on consumer spending.

Survey indicators such as small business hiring plans and employment indices have stabilised and improved since the 2025 weakness. Jobless claims show very limited layoffs. SEB expects a balanced labour market with low hiring and low firing.

macro_indicators.reading: 165k in the key points, 159k in the body text (estimate 70k)
macro_indicators.interpretation: The print beat all estimates and signals continued strong momentum. The report gives two different figures for the headline number.
The upward revision adds to the three-month pattern of upward revisions.
The decline reflects recovering participation and is consistent with a balanced labour market.
A partial reversal of the earlier downtrend linked to immigration policy.
Above expectations but consistent with the inflation target given productivity.
Modest wage growth means the labour market is not an inflation risk.
Below the pre-pandemic 180k-200k average, and slightly above SEB's estimated break-even of about 50k.
SEB's estimate of the monthly gain needed to keep unemployment stable, lowered by reduced immigration.

macro_indicators.reading: another rate hike, which SEB believes will be the final one
macro_indicators.interpretation: The jobs data supports the planned hike. Next week's CPI and equity market moves are the swing factors.

risk_factors: Sharp equity market declines and fading confidence in the AI expansion could lead the Fed to pause, because of the wealth effect on consumer spending. SEB says it would take much steeper declines to stop a December hike.
Monthly payroll data is highly volatile and heavily revised, so single months can mislead.
Hotter CPI next week would reinforce the case for tightening.
Households remain concerned about job availability.
geopolitical: Halted immigration, increased deportations and harsh immigration policies under President Trump have slowed labour force growth and cut participation. The participation decline has been only partly reversed.

tension_points.bull_case: Strong payrolls, upward revisions, lower unemployment and stabilising survey indicators support another and final hike in December.
tension_points.bear_case: Falling stock markets and fading confidence in the AI expansion could make the Fed pause because of wealth effects on consumer spending.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Much steeper equity market declines than currently seen, per SEB. Next week's CPI is the other key data point.
